summary:
North Dakota stands under the United States national framework in every respect that governs a trans visitor's documents, screening and entry. Executive Order 14168, signed 20 January 2025, redefined sex for federal purposes as a male-female binary, barred transgender people from government-funded single-sex facilities congruent with their gender identity, and prohibited self-selection of gender on passports and visas. The State Department has stopped processing the X marker and any marker inconsistent with sex assigned at birth, issues new passports only as M or F according to supporting documents, and leaves previously issued X-marker passports valid until they expire. The Supreme Court allowed those passport restrictions to take effect in November 2025, superseding a State Department policy in place since 1992. Trans and nonbinary travellers report passports confiscated or blocked at application, some left stranded abroad; the ACLU has sued the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs, and Lambda Legal maintains guidance on how name and gender changes interact with federal records.

North Dakota law independently closes the document route that a trans visitor may rely on at the state level. The 2023 statute tracked by the Movement Advancement Project bans all gender marker changes on birth certificates, with a narrow exception for individuals who have had genital surgery. The tracker marks North Dakota a negative law state, and a stricter and more explicit surgical requirement than applies in many other states. A July 2026 national anti-trans legal-risk assessment built from five years of daily legislative tracking places North Dakota among the worst states for legislation targeting transgender adults and among the states that prohibit any changes to birth certificates, a rule that forces trans people to out themselves when showing documents. The same assessment records that federal policies continue to create legal difficulties for transgender people nationwide.

Facilities access is restricted across a growing group of states: a Movement Advancement Project tally counts bathroom bans applying to trans people in K-12 schools and some government buildings in nine states and one territory, with outright state bans on facility use per gender identity elsewhere, and some states make trans bathroom use a criminal offence in certain circumstances. In April 2025 a transgender student was arrested and handcuffed in a women's restroom at the Florida state capitol, described by civil-rights attorneys as the first known arrest under that state's bathroom-restriction law. Screening inside the country carries an outing risk of its own, since TSA procedures can involve secondary screening, devices and pat-downs invasive of privacy; several foreign governments have responded, with advisories about trans people travelling to the United States issued from April 2025 and at least eight European countries adjusting entry guidelines for trans and nonbinary citizens by March 2025.
tangentialFactors:
Document rules elsewhere in the country have tightened further than North Dakota's. In February 2026 Kansas enacted a law preventing transgender people from changing markers on birth certificates and driver's licences, invalidating existing documents that do not match sex assigned at birth, and barring trans people from sex-segregated facilities; rights groups describe it as a template for other states, with further targeting bills pending in state legislatures. A July 2026 national risk assessment flagged Idaho as the latest Do Not Travel state for trans people, bringing the total to four states so flagged, and reported that the 2026 legislative season continued to degrade trans rights while federal policies drove nationwide trends.

Screening and visa processes at the border add exposure beyond state law. In February 2025 the State Department announced a ban on trans athletes entering the United States to compete in women's sports, flagging visa applicants with an internal marking and treating applicants who list a gender other than their assigned sex as grounds for a permanent fraud-based ban.

Trans-specific violence and custody harm are documented at federal level. From 2026 the Federal Bureau of Prisons adopted Florida-based policies mandating conversion therapy for transgender inmates, including cutting hair short, withdrawing hormone medication and substituting psychiatric therapy and drugs; the Bureau stopped reporting the number of transgender prisoners held from 2025. In immigration custody, transgender men were reportedly subjected to forced-labour programmes with refusals met by beatings, solitary confinement and reports of severe sexual abuse. In December 2025 the Attorney General instructed the FBI to offer cash bounties for information leading to the identification and arrest of transgender activists described as promoting radical gender ideology and characterised as domestic terrorist groups, and a May 2026 White House counterterrorism strategy stated that activities would prioritise the identification and neutralisation of groups whose ideology is anti-American, radically pro-transgender and anarchist. Advocates have compared these actions to the early stages of genocide.

Care access is constrained for visitors who need it. Executive Order 14187 of January 2025 described gender-affirming care for minors as chemical and surgical mutilation of children, leading some hospitals to pause care, and in summer 2025 the Department of Justice subpoenaed over 20 hospitals for full records of patients under 19. In July 2025 the federal government shut down specialised LGBTQ youth services on the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline; October 2025 proposed rules would bar Medicaid reimbursement for care to transgender patients under 18, and gender-affirming care for children is already banned in 27 states. Several of these federal measures have been blocked or enjoined in court, though the inventory does not identify which.
localsOnly:
North Dakota's enacted 2023 transgender-student statute, House Bill 1522, creates new sections of the North Dakota Century Code relating to preferred pronouns and providing accommodations to a transgender student. The bill carried a penalty provision and an emergency clause, passed through the 2023 regular session, and was signed by the governor, with the last official action filed with the Secretary of State on 9 May 2023.

For residents, the practical effect of the 2023 birth-certificate rule is that gender marker changes are unavailable except on proof of genital surgery, so identity documents held by trans residents remain aligned with sex assigned at birth. That aligns state records with the federal passport rule under which new documents are issued only as M or F, which means a resident's birth certificate, driver's licence and passport can generally be made consistent only in the direction of sex assigned at birth.

The Movement Advancement Project records federal policies as continuing to create legal difficulties for transgender people nationwide, a background condition residents face alongside state law rather than an alternative to it.
outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory does not resolve how the penalty provision attached to House Bill 1522 operates in practice: no enforcement cases, sanction amounts or administrative procedures are sourced, and whether the statute has been applied to anyone outside a school setting is not established here.

The narrow genital-surgery exception to the birth-certificate ban is stated by the Movement Advancement Project tracker but its evidentiary standard, processing times and actual grant rate in North Dakota are not sourced in this inventory.

North Dakota's driver's licence gender-marker rules are not covered by any source supplied here, so the licence position is unresolved rather than absent.

No North Dakota-specific facility, bathroom or restrooms law is documented in this inventory; the facility restrictions described come from national tallies and other states' statutes. Whether North Dakota has criminalised trans facility use, or declined to, is not sourced.

Enforcement data on document-related stops, refusals or outings of trans visitors in North Dakota is not sourced. The July 2026 assessment's classification of North Dakota as among the worst states is a rubric-based finding of that assessment, not a court finding or a government travel warning; the inventory does not place North Dakota among the four states flagged Do Not Travel in that assessment.

Which of the federal measures listed in the parent framework remain blocked, enjoined or in force as of writing is not specified by the sources, and that status is unresolved here.
